claims.claim: User research is the systematic gathering of information about users' needs, behaviors, and motivations, typically through observation, task analysis, and other feedback methodologies.
User research is the methodical study of target users, including their needs and pain points, so designers have sharper insights for design decisions.

Designing without research means guessing: teams that build from untested assumptions risk investing in features users do not actually need, and nearly all projects benefit from combining multiple research methods.
Interviews, surveys, observation (field studies), usability testing, and analytics are established user-research methods, each suited to different questions and stages of product development.

Qualitative research gathers data directly by observing or hearing people and answers why questions with depth from a small number of participants; quantitative research gathers data indirectly through instruments such as surveys or analytics tools and finds measurable patterns across many people.

Research happens throughout the product-development process: generative methods in early stages find new directions, formative methods improve the design during development, and summative methods measure performance after launch.

A leading question includes or implies the desired answer in its phrasing, and the researcher's wording can change what participants report; bias can enter research through researchers, participants, and methods.

Research reduces risk but does not eliminate it: qualitative findings point to problems, quantitative metrics need a reference point to interpret, and no single method or study can guarantee a design will succeed.

conflictingEvidence.detail: Usability.gov's archived definition centers on user behaviors, needs, and motivations gathered through observation, task analysis, and feedback methods, while IxDF's definition centers on the methodical study of target users' needs and pain points. Both describe the same practice; the lesson uses the needs-behaviors-motivations formulation as its attributed working definition.

NN/g notes that what people say and what people do often differ, and that self-reported data is limited by what people are aware of and willing to report. The lesson therefore presents observation and analytics as complements to interviews and surveys rather than as replacements for them.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-1 draft contained only generic boilerplate (e.g., 'User Research is a foundational concept in Ux/Ui Design') with no sourceable claims; it was fully rewritten for phase 2.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft with a scoped, source-verified lesson; added an attributed working definition, original examples, and verified claims about methods, qual/quant, timing, and bias.
rightsIssues: All five sources were used reference-only; no source prose was reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: When to Use Which User-Experience Research Methods
sourceRecords.license: Copyright NN/g; used as reference only
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports: research methods span qualitative-quantitative and attitudinal-behavioral dimensions; interviews, surveys, field studies, usability testing, and analytics are established methods; qualitative data is gathered directly by observing or hearing people while quantitative data is gathered indirectly through instruments such as surveys or analytics tools; methods map to product-development stages (generative/strategize, formative/design, summative/launch-and-assess); nearly all projects benefit from multiple methods and from combining insights. No source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Quantitative vs. Qualitative Usability Testing
sourceRecords.license: Copyright NN/g; used as reference only
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports: qualitative data are observational findings identifying which design features are easy or hard to use; quantitative data are metrics such as task-completion rates and task times; the two play complementary roles in an iterative design cycle; quantitative results are numbers that need a reference point (a baseline, competitor, or previous design) to interpret meaningfully. No source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Leading Questions in User Research
sourceRecords.license: Copyright NN/g; used as reference only
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports: a leading question includes or implies the desired answer in its phrasing; the facilitator's choice of words can affect participants' feedback; neutral framing (e.g., asking what was easy or difficult about reaching content) yields more reliable responses than phrasing that names an assumed problem. No source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is User Research?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports: user research as the methodical study of target users' needs and pain points; research can be applied at any point in the design process; teams typically begin with qualitative measures to discover needs and motivations and later test with quantitative measures; quantitative methods such as surveys gather measurable data from large samples to find patterns; bias can enter research through researchers, participants, and methods. No source prose reproduced.
